unit.title: Operate in an autonomous team environment

summary: This unit is about working in an electrical crew that plans and runs much of its own work with little direct supervision. You will learn how such a team sets targets, shares out tasks and roles, keeps everyone safe (including group isolation), develops its members' skills, communicates with clients and other trades, settles disagreements, solves problems, and measures and reports its performance.

blocks.p: Many electrical jobs are done by small crews that work on their own for days at a time: a housing scheme, a school rewire, a factory shutdown. The manager sets the targets and the limits; the crew decides how to reach them. This is an **autonomous** (self-managed) team. At Level 3 you are expected to be a full member of such a team and, often, to lead parts of its work: planning, sharing tasks, coaching newer members, checking quality and reporting.

blocks.h: What you must be able to do

head: Task
What it looks like on the job
rows: Understand how a self-managed team works
Know what the team decides for itself, what it must refer to the manager or designer, and how its work fits the company's plans.
Plan the team's work
Break a job into tasks, set clear targets, estimate time and materials, and track progress on a chart or board.
Share tasks and roles fairly
Use a skills matrix to match people to tasks, rotate roles, and pair less experienced members with skilled ones.
Keep the team safe
Apply group isolation with a multi-lock hasp, follow permits, hold toolbox talks, stop unsafe work, and act in an emergency.
Develop team members
Coach, give constructive feedback, record progress on the skills matrix, and help a member who is struggling.
Communicate well
Run short, useful meetings, hand over work clearly, keep the client informed, and coordinate with other trades.
Work through team development and conflict
Recognise the stages a team goes through, treat everyone with respect, and settle disagreements on the facts.
Solve problems and improve the work
Collect facts, find root causes with simple tools, try changes on a small scale and keep a lessons-learned log.
Measure and report performance
Track simple measures such as right-first-time and output, review them as a team, and report progress and problems early.

blocks.note: A self-managed team still works inside the law, the electrical code, the company's rules, the drawings and the specification. 'Self-managed' means the crew organises **how** the work is done, not that it can change **what** has been designed or skip safety rules.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.note: Jamaican contractors often work on housing schemes, schools, clinics, hotels and factories in occupied buildings, where staff, guests or patients are still present. The crew is a guest in those buildings: respect, tidiness and clear warnings before any shutdown matter as much as good wiring.
blocks.label: Jamaica

sections.title: How a self-managed electrical team works

blocks.p: In a closely supervised team a foreman decides who does what each day. In a self-managed team the members decide together, within targets, budgets and rules set by management. The manager becomes a coach and a link to the rest of the company, not a daily boss.

blocks.h: Why it can work better, and what can go wrong

head: Benefits
Risks
How the team controls the risk
rows: Problems are solved quickly, on the spot, by the people who know the job
The team makes a decision that is not its to make, such as changing the design
Agree in writing what the team may decide and what it must refer up
Members take ownership and pride in the work
Some members do less and others carry them
Clear tasks with names and dates; fair sharing; reviews of who did what
Skills spread as members train each other
Safety slips because everyone thinks someone else is checking
A named safety lead on a rota; checks recorded; anyone may stop unsafe work
The team adapts its plan fast when the site changes
Arguments drag on with no way to settle them
Ground rules for settling disagreements, and a route to the manager

blocks.p: Every self-managed team needs to know where its authority ends. A common split is:

head: The team usually decides
The team refers to the manager, designer or client
rows: The order of work each day
Who does which task, and pairings for training
How to share tools and the van
Meeting times and the rota for roles
Small improvements to its own methods
Any change to the design: cable sizes, protective devices, circuit numbers, positions shown on the drawing
Extra work or changes the client asks for (variations), and their cost
Delays that will move the finish date
Defects found in existing installations, such as a missing earthing conductor
Discipline, pay and hiring

blocks.note: If the team finds something outside its authority, such as an existing installation with no main earthing conductor, it stops any work affected by it, makes the area safe, records what it found (with photos) and reports it at once. It does not quietly fix it, and it does not ignore it.
blocks.label: Safety

blocks.p: A new team agrees a short set of ground rules at the start and writes them down. Typical items: start and finish times; how and when the team meets; how decisions are made; how disagreements are settled; who speaks to the client; safety rules that are never negotiable (such as proving dead every time); keeping the work area tidy; and how the team reports to the manager. Everyone signs, and the rules are reviewed when they stop working.

head: Role
What it involves
rows: Coordinator (team leader for the week or the job)
Runs the meetings, keeps the plan and the progress board up to date, and is the link to the manager.
Safety lead
Checks permits, isolations, first-aid kit, extinguishers and access equipment; leads toolbox talks. Often rotated so that every member learns the duty and nobody gets careless.
Inspector or checker
Checks completed work against the drawing and the check sheet before testing, and initials it. Never checks their own work.
Planner
Works out materials and orders them in time; books shared equipment such as test instruments.
Client contact
The one person who speaks for the team to the client, so the client gets one clear message.
Installers and testers
Do the work, record it and test it. Everyone in the team does this as well as any other role.

blocks.p: A **RACI chart** lists the team's main tasks down the side and the people across the top. Each box gets a letter:

head: Letter
Meaning
Example: 'test and record the new circuits'
rows: R
**Responsible**: does the task
The two members who test
A
**Accountable**: answers for it being done right, and signs it off (only one person)
The team's Level 3 coordinator
C
**Consulted**: asked for their views before or during the task
The designer, if a result is unclear
I
**Informed**: told the result
The manager and the client

blocks.p: Who answers for a test result? The member who carried out the test answers for doing it properly and recording it honestly, and the member who checked it answers for the check. That is why both sign or initial the record.

blocks.note: The team's targets must fit the company's wider plans: its budget, its promises to clients and its safety rules. A crew that finishes early by cutting corners, or that 'wins' a disagreement with another crew by taking their tester, has not helped the business.
blocks.label: Remember

sections.title: Planning the work, targets and resources

blocks.p: A self-managed team plans its own work. Good planning is the difference between a calm job and a scramble.

flow: Read the drawings, specification and programme, and walk the site
Break the job into tasks in the order they must be done
Estimate time and labour for each task from past records
Share tasks by skills, with pairs for training
Work out materials and book shared equipment
Set targets and show the plan on a chart or board
Check progress daily and re-plan early when things change

head: Letter
Means
Example
rows: S
Specific: says exactly what
First fix of lighting and outlets in Block C, ground floor
M
Measurable: you can count it
All 36 boxes fixed and conduit in
A
Achievable: possible with the people and time
Checked against past rates: about 12 boxes a day for a pair
R
Relevant: helps the job and the company
The plasterers start Block C on Monday
T
Time-bound: has a deadline
By Friday at 3 p.m.

blocks.p: 'Get Block C done soon' is not a target. 'Fix all 36 boxes and conduit in Block C ground floor by Friday 3 p.m.' is: everyone knows what done looks like and when.

ul: Use the team's own records: if job sheets show that terminating a distribution board always takes twice as long as planned, find out why and plan future boards with the real figure.
Allow for things that always happen: deliveries, inspections, other trades in the way, weather on outdoor work.
Add the time for testing, snagging and paperwork. These are part of the job, not extras.

blocks.p: A **Gantt chart** shows each task as a horizontal bar along a timeline. Bars that depend on each other are drawn in order: cables cannot be drawn in until the conduit is in, and testing cannot start until the cables are terminated. If an early task slips, every task that depends on it slips too, unless the team re-plans (for example by starting the next task in areas that are ready). A **progress board** (a whiteboard or flip chart on site) shows the week's targets, what is done and who is doing what, and is updated at the end of each day.

ul: Shared equipment, such as the only insulation resistance tester or a scaffold tower, is booked in a log with agreed times. When two teams need the same item, the leaders agree the times and record them, rather than whoever gets there first taking it.
Materials are worked out early and ordered in time, so the job is never held up for a box of outlets.
Tools and test instruments are signed out and back, and faults are reported.

blocks.p: A **site diary** is kept every day: who was on site, the work done, deliveries, visitors, instructions received (and from whom), problems, delays and their causes, weather, and any accidents or near misses. It is the team's memory. When there is a dispute about a delay or an instruction weeks later, the diary settles it.

When the team sees that it will miss a date, for example because the client has added circuits or materials are late, it tells the manager **at once**, with the reason and a realistic new date. Bad news reported early can be managed; bad news found on the deadline cannot.
With no supervisor watching, safety depends on every member. The team must have clear rules, named duties and the confidence to stop work.

blocks.h: Group isolation: one board, several workers

blocks.p: When several people work on circuits from the same board or isolator, each needs their own protection. A **multi-lock hasp** is clipped onto the isolator handle; it has several holes, and the isolator cannot be switched on until every padlock has been removed from it.

flow: Agree which board and circuits are to be worked on, and warn the people affected
One member switches off the isolator and fits the multi-lock hasp
Each worker fits their own padlock and danger tag (name, date, reason) and keeps their own key
A tester is proved on a proving unit, every conductor pair is tested dead, and the tester is proved again
Work starts only now
Each worker removes only their own lock, when their own work is finished and safe
The supply is restored only when every lock is off and the team has checked everyone is clear

ul: Never lend your key or use someone else's lock. A lock protects only the person who fitted it.
A worker who leaves site removes their own lock first, after making their work safe and telling the coordinator. The others' locks stay on.

If a lock is left on and its owner has gone (for example home with the key), nobody cuts it off. The company's **lock-removal procedure** is followed: try to contact the owner, the supervisor checks that nobody is working on the circuits and that it is safe, the removal is authorised and recorded, and the owner is told before their next shift.
Some sites use a **group lock box**: the isolation keys go in a box and each worker locks the box with their own padlock.

blocks.p: On many industrial and commercial sites, high-risk work (live testing, work near high voltage, hot work, confined spaces) needs a **permit to work**: written permission, issued by an authorised person, that says exactly what may be done, by whom, where, when and with which precautions. The team works within it and hands it back when finished.

blocks.h: When something is not as expected

head: Situation
What the team does
rows: A tester shows voltage on a circuit everyone believed was dead
Stop. Warn the whole team. Nobody touches anything until the source is found (a wrong label, a second supply, a borrowed neutral) and isolated, and the circuit is proved dead again.
A member finds a damaged lead or tool
Take it out of use, tag it 'Do not use', and report it. Do not leave it for someone else to pick up.
A member is tired at the end of a long day before careful work, such as terminating a board
Leave it until the morning if possible. Tired people make more mistakes in careful work.
Hot roof or outdoor work in the Jamaican sun
Plan it for cooler hours, rotate people, provide water and shade, and watch for signs of heat exhaustion.
A new member joins, perhaps from another trade
Before they work on any circuit, they must know the team's isolation and lock-off procedure, the emergency arrangements and the site rules. Give them a buddy.

blocks.p: In an emergency, such as a fire or an electric shock, there is no time for discussion: one person (the nearest competent member, or whoever the plan names) takes charge and gives clear instructions, and the others follow them. If someone is still in contact with a live conductor, **switch off the supply without touching them**; if you cannot, push them clear with a dry non-conducting object. Then call for help (110 for ambulance and fire in Jamaica), and start first aid. The team should know who its first-aiders are and where the kit and extinguishers are; checking them is a duty on the rota.

ul: A **toolbox talk** is a short safety talk on site, often before work starts, about one hazard: ladders, safe isolation, heat, dust, a recent near miss. Members take turns to give them.
Anyone in the team may **stop work** they believe is unsafe, without blame, until it is sorted out.

Make it clear that every concern will be heard. A member who thinks the plan is unsafe but is afraid to say so is a danger to everyone. Thank people for raising concerns, even when they turn out to be wrong.

blocks.note: Safe isolation is never put to a vote. If a member says proving dead 'wastes time', the circuit stays untouched until the procedure is followed, and the reasons are explained. If the member still refuses, the team reports it to the manager.
blocks.label: Safety

blocks.p: A strong team does not depend on one person. It spreads skills so that work does not stop when someone is away, and so that every member can grow.
A **skills matrix** is a chart with the team's members down one side and the skills the work needs across the top. Each box shows the member's level.

head: Skill
Annalise
Delroy
Marlon
Sheree
rows: Conduit bending and fixing
Terminating distribution boards
Insulation and continuity testing
Armoured cable glands
Lighting control programming

blocks.p: Levels in this example: 1 = not trained; 2 = can do it with supervision; 3 = can do it alone; 4 = can do it alone and teach others. The matrix shows at a glance that only Delroy can terminate armoured cable glands and only Marlon can set up the lighting control. If either is off sick, that work stops. The team should plan to train a second member in each, during the job, by pairing them with the expert.

ul: Review the matrix **before** taking on a new type of job, such as solar PV or a fire alarm system, to find the gaps and plan training in good time.
Use it to share tasks fairly, so that everyone gets to do the skilled work as well as the routine work.
Update it as members are trained, so the team knows when someone can work alone.

flow: Plan when, so the job's timing allows it
Explain the task and why each step matters
Show it slowly, on an off-cut or practice piece
Let the member do it while you watch and ask questions
Give clear feedback: what is good, what to change
Check their real work before it is closed up or tested
Increase their independence step by step and record progress

blocks.p: Coaching while the job goes on builds skills without risking quality, because the experienced member checks the work before it is covered or energised.

head: Good feedback is
Example
rows: Specific: about a particular piece of work
'Three of your ferrule numbers in panel 2 don't match the drawing.' not 'Your labelling is sloppy.'
About the work, not the person
'The neutral in outlet 4 was loose.' not 'You're careless.'
Balanced: says what is good, too
'Your cable runs are neat and well supported.'
Timely: soon after the work
The same day, while the member remembers it and can act on it, not weeks later
Private, when it is a correction
A quiet word, not in front of the client or the rest of the team
Two-way
Ask for their view, and agree what happens next

blocks.p: Feedback that helps a person improve, rather than only criticising, is called **constructive** feedback.

blocks.h: When a member's work keeps failing

blocks.p: If a member's work keeps failing inspection, the first step is a private conversation, not a public telling-off. Find out why: unclear instructions, a skill they were never taught, wrong tools, a problem at home, or poor eyesight for small terminals. Agree support (coaching, a buddy, a checklist) and a time to review. If there is still no improvement, or the problem is unsafe behaviour, the team refers it to the manager.

ul: Share tasks by skill and by the need to learn, not by gender, age, where someone comes from or who is friends with whom. A female member who is always given the paperwork, or a young member who always gets the cleaning, is being held back.
Teasing about someone's accent, home district, appearance or religion is not 'just fun' if it hurts or excludes them. Deal with it early and privately; if it continues, report it.
People who feel respected speak up, including about safety. People who feel picked on keep quiet.

sections.title: Communication: meetings, handovers, clients and other trades

blocks.p: A short meeting at the start of each day (often 10 to 15 minutes, standing up) keeps everyone on the same plan. A useful agenda:

ol: Yesterday: what was finished, and any problems.
Today: the tasks, who does each, and the targets.
Today's hazards and controls: isolations, who holds each lock, access equipment, other trades nearby, weather.
Materials, tools and test instruments needed.
Anything to report to the manager or client.

blocks.p: Keep it short with a set agenda and a time limit. Longer team meetings (weekly reviews, planning) end with an **action list**: each action agreed, who will do it and by when. Without that, the same problems are discussed again next week.
Work often passes from one pair to another, or from one day to the next. A poor handover is a common cause of accidents: someone assumes a circuit is complete, or dead, when it is not.

ul: Label unfinished work clearly at the point of work, for example 'NOT COMPLETE: neutrals not terminated', and leave it safe: isolated, locked off if needed, conductor ends insulated, covers on.
Brief the next pair face to face where possible, and write it in the handover log or site diary: what is done, what is not, the state of isolations and any hazards.
The person taking over checks for themselves. They never assume a circuit is dead because someone said so.
Agree one **client contact** for the team, so the client hears one clear message.
Give regular updates: what is done, what is next, any problems such as late materials.
Warn the client in good time before any shutdown, and agree the time, especially where there are fridges, computers, medical equipment or guests.

In an occupied home or business, respect the property: protect floors and furniture, keep the work area clean and safe at the end of each day, keep children and pets away from work, and keep noise and dust down.

When the client asks for a change (an extra outlet, a moved light), the member asked does not just agree. It goes to the team leader, who checks it is safe and allowed, prices the extra time and material, and agrees it in writing as a **variation** before the work is done. The change is marked on the drawings.
Find out the site rules and the overall programme from the site manager, and attend the coordination meetings.
Fit the electrical work into the sequence: conduit and boxes in walls before plastering, cables drawn in after the roof is on so they stay dry, final fixes after painting.

Agree routes early with plumbers, air-conditioning fitters and gas fitters, using the drawings, so services do not clash. If another trade plans to cut through your route, meet them, check the drawings and agree a solution.
Never energise a circuit for another trade until it has been tested and handed over, and never let another trade switch on your circuits.
Report problems, such as damage to your work, to the site manager with facts and photos, rather than arguing on site.

blocks.note: Respect and clear communication with clients and other trades save more time than any short cut. A crew that is known for keeping people informed gets the next job.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: Most new teams go through recognisable stages (described by Bruce Tuckman). Knowing them helps you understand what is happening and what helps.

head: Stage
What you see
What helps
rows: Forming
Members are polite and cautious, unsure of their roles, and look to the leader or manager for direction.
Clear goals, roles and ground rules; introductions; early, simple tasks.
Storming
Disagreements over methods, roles and who leads; members challenge each other and test the rules.
Bring disagreements into the open; settle them on facts; restate the goals and ground rules; do not take sides.
Norming
The team agrees its ways of working; members accept each other's roles and start to trust each other.
Write down what works; share leadership roles; encourage feedback.
Performing
The team works well together with little supervision, solves its own problems and meets its targets.
Give the team freedom within its limits; stretch it with new skills; recognise good work.
Adjourning
The job ends and the team breaks up or moves on.
Review the job, record lessons learned and recognise everyone's part.

blocks.p: Teams can slip back a stage when a member leaves or joins, or when the job changes. Storming is normal and can be useful if it is handled well: it is how the team finds the best way of working.

ul: Different views on how to do the work, such as which route a conduit should take.
Unfair sharing of work, or someone seen to be doing less.
Unclear roles: two people both think they are in charge.
Pressure of deadlines, heat and long hours.
Blame after a mistake, especially in front of a client.
Personal differences and disrespect.

head: Approach
What it looks like
When it fits
rows: Avoiding
Ignoring the problem and hoping it goes away
Only for trivial matters; real problems usually grow
Accommodating
One side gives way to keep the peace
When the issue matters much more to the other person
Competing
One side insists on its view
When safety or the law is at stake: safe isolation is not negotiable
Compromising
Each side gives up something to reach agreement
When time is short and both views have merit
Collaborating
Both sides work together to find the best answer for the job
Usually the best for the team when there is time to do it

flow: Stop a public argument at once, especially in front of a client
Take it somewhere private, when tempers have cooled
Let each person explain their view without interruption
Look at the facts: the drawing, the specification, the records
Agree a way forward and what each person will do
Follow up later; refer it to the manager if it is not settled

blocks.note: Argue about the work, never about the person. 'This route needs four extra bends' can be settled with a tape measure; 'You always want things your way' cannot.
blocks.label: Tip

ul: Work to the drawing, the specification and the code, every time.

Use a **check sheet** on which a second member, who did not do the work, checks each circuit (terminations tight, conductors identified, cables supported and protected, labels correct) and initials it. Faults are caught early, before testing or before the work is covered, and the check is recorded.
Record test results honestly. A result is written only for a test that was done, by the person who did it.

flow: Define the problem clearly: what, where, when, how often
Collect the facts: readings, records, what people saw
List the possible causes
Test the likely causes safely, one at a time
Fix the root cause
Check that the fix worked
Change the way of working so it does not happen again

blocks.p: The biggest mistake is to jump to a cure before collecting the facts. If several new circuits fail their insulation test, find out which circuits, what readings and which routes they share before anybody starts pulling cables out.

head: Tool
How it works
Example
rows: Tally chart and Pareto
Count how often each kind of fault happens and list them from the most to the least common. Usually a few causes give most of the faults.
A month's inspection faults: the top one or two types are tackled first, especially if they are also a safety risk.
Cause-and-effect (fishbone) diagram
Write the problem at the 'head', and sort possible causes into groups along the 'bones': people, methods, materials, equipment, environment.
Why outlets fail polarity checks: training (people), no check sheet (methods), wrong colour cable delivered (materials)…
Five whys
Ask 'why?' about the problem, then about the answer, and so on, until you reach a cause you can fix.
Cables nicked → pulled over sharp box edges → no bushes fitted → bushes not on the material list. Fix: add bushes to the standard list.

blocks.h: Trying a change: Plan, Do, Check, Act

blocks.p: When a member suggests a better method, such as making up earth fly-leads on the bench before going to site, the team does not adopt or reject it on opinion. It uses **PDCA**: **Plan** the change and how to measure it; **Do** it on a small scale, such as one floor or a few houses; **Check** the results against the old way; **Act**: adopt it everywhere if it worked, or try something else if it did not.

A **lessons-learned log** records good ideas and mistakes from each job, so that they are used on the next one. At the end of a job the team holds a short **review** (debrief): what went well, what went badly, and what to do differently. It is about the work, not about blaming people.
A team that does not measure its work cannot tell whether it is improving. The measures should be few, simple and understood by everyone.

head: Measure
How it is worked out
What it tells the team
rows: Right first time
Circuits passing all tests first time ÷ circuits tested × 100
Quality of workmanship; fewer failures means less rework
Output
Points, boxes or circuits completed ÷ days
Whether the team is on track for its targets
Schedule
Tasks finished on time ÷ tasks due
How good the planning and estimates are
Rework
Hours spent putting right faulty work
The cost of poor quality
Callbacks
Faults reported by clients after handover
Quality as the client sees it
Near misses reported
Count per month
A leading safety measure: it shows problems before someone is hurt
Injuries
Count per month or year
A lagging safety measure: it counts harm after it has happened

blocks.p: **Example.** A team wired 108 points in 4 days: an average of 108 ÷ 4 = 27 points a day. If its target is 30 a day, it is behind and should find out why.

ul: Look for patterns, not just totals. If output drops every Monday, look at what is different on Mondays: late material deliveries, a long journey, time spent setting up after the weekend.
Compare like with like: a day of testing will not produce many new points.
A rise in near-miss reports is often a good sign: it means people feel safe to report.
Review the figures together, without blame, and agree actions, each with an owner and a date. Check next month whether the actions worked.

blocks.p: A short regular report (often weekly) keeps the manager informed: progress against the plan, the measures, problems and what the team is doing about them, things the team needs (materials, decisions, people), and any safety events. Report delays, variations and safety concerns as soon as they arise, not just in the weekly report.

blocks.note: Measures are for improving the work, not for punishing people. If members fear the figures, they will hide problems, and the figures will stop telling the truth.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: Tick each statement only when you can do it without looking at the notes.

ul: I can explain what a self-managed team is, its benefits and its risks.
I can say which decisions the team makes and which it must refer to the manager, designer or client.
I can describe common team roles and use a RACI chart.
I can break a job into tasks, set SMART targets and show the plan on a Gantt chart or progress board.
I can explain what happens to later tasks when an early task slips.
I can carry out group isolation with a multi-lock hasp and explain why each worker uses their own lock.
I can describe what happens when a lock is left on and its owner has gone.
I can say what the team does when voltage is found on a circuit believed dead, or when a defect outside its authority is found.
I can use a skills matrix to share work and plan training.
I can coach a member through a new task and give constructive feedback.
I can run a short start-of-day meeting and hand over unfinished work safely.
I can keep a client informed and handle a change request as a variation.
I can coordinate with other trades and the site manager.
I can name the stages of team development and say what helps at each stage.
I can help settle a disagreement on the facts and deal with disrespect.
I can use a tally chart, a fishbone diagram and five whys to find causes.
I can use Plan-Do-Check-Act to try an improvement.
I can work out simple performance measures and review them with the team.

terms: Autonomous (self-managed) team
A team that plans and organises its own work within targets and limits set by management.
Constructive feedback
Specific, timely comments on work that help a person improve.
Debrief (review)
A short meeting at the end of a job to look at what went well and what to improve.
Fishbone diagram
A cause-and-effect diagram that sorts possible causes of a problem into groups.
Gantt chart
A chart showing tasks as horizontal bars along a timeline.
Ground rules
The ways of working a team agrees and writes down at the start.
Lagging measure
A measure of harm or results after the event, such as injuries.
Leading measure
A measure that warns of problems before harm, such as near misses reported.
Lessons-learned log
A record of good ideas and mistakes from each job, for use on the next.
Limits of authority
The boundary between what the team may decide and what it must refer up.
Lock-removal procedure
The authorised, recorded way to remove a lock whose owner is not present.
Multi-lock hasp
A fitting with several holes clipped onto an isolator so each worker can add their own padlock.
Pareto (tally) analysis
Counting faults by type to find the few causes that give most of the problems.
PDCA
Plan, Do, Check, Act: a cycle for trying and adopting improvements.
Permit to work
Written permission, from an authorised person, for stated high-risk work under stated precautions.
RACI chart
A chart of who is Responsible, Accountable, Consulted and Informed for each task.
Right first time
The share of work that passes inspection and tests at the first attempt.
Site diary
A daily record of work, people, instructions, problems and events on site.
Skills matrix
A chart showing which team members have which skills, and at what level.
SMART target
A target that is Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant and Time-bound.
Toolbox talk
A short safety talk to the team on site about one hazard.
Variation
A change to the agreed work that must be agreed and priced before it is done.

c1.title: Rewiring a clinic in Chapelton
c1.text: A self-managed crew of five (Rohan, a Level 3 electrician who is coordinator this month, with Annalise, Delroy, Marlon and Sheree) has three weeks to rewire a health clinic in Chapelton, Clarendon, while it stays open. Wing B is fed from board DB-2, which also supplies the vaccine fridge. The crew's Gantt chart shows conduit in Wing B on days 1 to 4, cable pulling on days 5 to 7, terminations on days 8 and 9 and testing on day 10. For work on DB-2, the crew uses a multi-lock hasp on its isolator.

c2.title: A new crew at a Liguanea apartment block
c2.text: Four electricians from two companies were put together three weeks ago to wire an apartment block in Liguanea, St Andrew. Kemar and Dwight, both Level 3, argue often about conduit routes and about which of them should lead. The tidy-up rota the crew agreed in the first week is being ignored. Dwight regularly jokes about the accent of Tyrone, the youngest member, who grew up in rural St Elizabeth.

c3.title: Test failures at a Lionel Town housing scheme
c3.text: A self-managed crew is wiring 60 houses at a scheme in Lionel Town, Clarendon. Last month it tested 168 circuits, and 21 failed their first test: 11 loose neutral terminals at the boards, 6 insulation faults where cables were nicked entering steel boxes, 3 wrong breaker sizes and 1 missing protective conductor. With the handover date close, Garfield suggests recording 'pass' for the last ten circuits, which he is 'sure are fine', and testing them later.

c4.title: A hotel kitchen upgrade in Oracabessa
c4.text: A crew is upgrading the electrical supply to a hotel kitchen in Oracabessa, St Mary, during a two-week closure. Refrigeration technicians want power to the new walk-in cooler's board before the crew has tested it. Two members must run cable tray on the kitchen's flat concrete roof. On day 3, a member drilling a fixing hole felt the drill hit metal behind the tiles and stopped: it was a gas pipe, not shown on the electrical drawing.

c5.title: A new member at a Twickenham Park factory
c5.text: Joel, a qualified plumber retraining as an electrician, has joined the maintenance crew at a bottling factory in Twickenham Park, St Catherine. Natalie, a Level 3 electrician, is his buddy. Joel's control-panel wiring is neat, but several of his ferrule numbers do not match the drawing. Natalie has twice seen him test for dead without first proving his tester on the proving unit.

questions.q: On day 3 Delroy finishes his part early and must leave site. What should he do about his padlock on the DB-2 hasp?
o: Leave it on, so the board stays locked off until he is back
Give his key to Sheree so she can take the lock off later
Tell Rohan, leave his work safe and remove only his lock
Remove all the locks, then refit the ones still needed
questions.why: A lock protects only the person who fitted it, and only while they are working. Leaving it on would hold up the others and force the lock-removal procedure later; handing over a key defeats the system. The others' locks stay on until each of them has finished.

questions.q: The conduit in Wing B is running two days late. If the crew changes nothing, what happens to its plan?
o: The tasks that follow it slip too, unless the crew re-plans
Only the conduit is late; the tasks after it keep their dates
Testing can still go ahead on day 10, before the cables are in
The finish is safe, as a Gantt chart shows bars, not links
questions.why: Cables cannot be pulled until the conduit is in, and terminating and testing follow the cables, so a slip in the first task pushes the rest back. The crew can recover, for example by pulling cables in rooms where conduit is finished or adding a person, and must tell the client early if the finish date is at risk.

questions.q: Delroy reads the new steriliser's rating plate and is sure the cable size on the drawing is too small for it. What should the crew do?
o: Fit a bigger cable, since the crew is self-managed and he is right
Fit the size on the drawing, since the design has been approved
Vote at the morning meeting and fit the size most members choose
Hold that circuit and refer it to the designer via the manager
questions.why: A cable size is a design decision, outside a self-managed crew's authority, even when the crew may be right. Installing a size you believe is unsafe is just as wrong. Hold that circuit, give the designer the rating-plate figures and your working, and record the answer before going on.

questions.q: How should the crew plan the times when DB-2 must be switched off?
o: Switch off when the crew is ready; the fridge can wait an hour
Agree each shutdown with the clinic in advance, with notice
Let each pair switch off when it needs to, to avoid waiting
Switch off at lunch each day, when fewer patients are in
questions.why: Patients, staff and the vaccine fridge depend on the supply. Shutdowns are planned with the person in charge of the building, at agreed times, with notice and a plan for critical loads such as the fridge. One member coordinates them, so pairs never switch off without warning.

questions.q: On the RACI chart for 'agreeing shutdown times', Rohan arranges them, the manager signs them off, and the nurse-in-charge gives her views before they are fixed. Which letter belongs in her box?
o: R
A
C
I
questions.why: She is Consulted: asked for her views before the decision. Rohan does the task (Responsible), the manager answers for it and signs it off (Accountable), and staff who only need to be told the times are Informed.

questions.q: Which stage of team development is the Liguanea crew most likely to be in?
o: Forming
Norming
Adjourning
Storming
questions.why: Storming is when members challenge each other and the leadership, argue over methods and roles, and test the agreed rules. It is normal and can be worked through by settling roles and ground rules. Forming is the polite, cautious start; norming comes when the team settles its ways; adjourning is the break-up at the end.

questions.q: Kemar and Dwight each want a different conduit route for the riser. What is the best way for the crew to settle it?
o: Compare both on the drawing, materials and access, then agree
Let the more senior of the two decide, so work can carry on
Ask the client to pick one, since it is the client's building
Use one route on each floor, so that neither of them loses face
questions.why: A decision based on facts (the drawing, the specification, materials, labour, access for future maintenance) settles the argument on merit, not on who wins. If either route changes what the drawing shows, the designer decides. Mixing routes to keep the peace gives an untidy, inconsistent job.

questions.q: Dwight says his jokes about Tyrone's accent are 'just fun'. What should a Level 3 member of the crew do?
o: Leave it, since Tyrone has not complained to anybody
Tell Dwight privately that it stops, and check on Tyrone
Tell Tyrone to laugh along, so that he fits in with the crew
Report Dwight to the manager at once, without a word to him
questions.why: Jokes about where someone comes from or how they speak are disrespect, and they usually get worse if nobody speaks up. A member who feels picked on stops speaking up, including about safety. Deal with it early and privately; if it carries on, take it to the manager.

questions.q: The tidy-up rota is being ignored, and off-cuts are piling up on the stairs. What is the best first step?
o: Ask the manager to fine any member who misses his turn on the rota
Give the job to Tyrone, as the newest member of the crew
Clear the stairs now, then agree a fix for the rota together
Leave it until the end of the job, when there will be more time
questions.why: Off-cuts on stairs are a trip hazard today, so they are cleared now. Ground rules then only work if the team owns them: raise it openly, find out why the rota is failing and agree a fix. Giving the job to the newest member is unfair, and fines are not the team's decision.

questions.q: What was the crew's right-first-time rate last month?
questions.why: Right first time = circuits passing first time ÷ circuits tested × 100 = 147 ÷ 168 × 100 = 87.5%. 12.5% is the failure rate. 85.7% and 14.3% come from dividing by 147 instead of by all 168 circuits tested. Tracking this figure each month shows whether the crew's changes are working.

questions.q: Asking 'why?' about the nicked cables, the crew finds: cables were pulled over sharp knockout edges, because no bushes were fitted, because bushes were left off the standard material list. What should it fix?
o: The material list, so bushes come with each order
The damaged cables, then carry on as before
The pulling speed, by telling members to slow down
The testing order, so faults show up sooner
questions.why: Asking 'why?' until you reach a cause you can fix stops the fault coming back. Replacing the nicked cables cures these six circuits only; adding bushes to the standard list (and to the box check sheet) prevents it in every house still to be wired.

questions.q: The crew tries a second-person check of board terminations on 10 houses for two weeks, then compares their failures with houses without the check. Which step of Plan-Do-Check-Act is that comparison?
o: Plan
Check
Do
Act
questions.why: Plan the change, Do it on a small scale, Check the results against the old way, then Act: adopt it on every house if it worked, or try something else. Trying it on a few houses first limits the cost if the idea does not work.

questions.q: What should the crew do about Garfield's suggestion for the last ten circuits?
o: Agree, as long as Garfield signs for the ten circuits himself
Agree, and test them quietly in the week after handover
Refuse; test them, or tell the manager the date is at risk
Record 'pass' only for the circuits Garfield installed himself
questions.why: A test record says that a test was done and what it showed. Writing results for tests not done falsifies a safety record: a house could be energised with a fault, and everyone who signed is answerable. Do the tests, or report the delay early with a realistic new date.

questions.q: What should the crew tell the refrigeration technicians who want power to the cooler's board?
o: It can go on now, as they only need it for a short test
They may switch it on themselves, since it only feeds their cooler
It can go on now, if a warning notice is put on the board
It stays off until tested; the site manager will agree a time
questions.why: A circuit is energised only after its dead tests pass and the crew hands it over. Agreeing a time through the site manager lets the refrigeration firm plan its work. Another trade must never switch on an electrical crew's circuits.

questions.q: Which plan is best for the cable tray work on the flat roof?
o: Work in cooler hours, take turns, and keep water and shade
Do it in one long push at midday to get it over with quickly
Send the two youngest members, as they cope better with heat
Work through lunch, so the roof job takes the fewest hours
questions.why: Heat on a Jamaican concrete roof makes people slow, careless and ill. Planning the hottest work for cooler hours, sharing it out, and taking breaks in shade with water keeps people safe and the work accurate. Age is no protection against heat illness.

questions.q: What should the crew do after the drill hit the gas pipe?
o: Carry on, since the pipe held and nobody was hurt
Stop, report it and check routes with the gas fitter
Move the fixing 100 mm along, and carry on without a fuss
Warn the member privately, so the hotel does not find out
questions.why: A near miss shows the method failed: the pipe's route was unknown. Stop, have the pipe checked for damage, report it, and agree how to find other services (drawings, a detector, asking the other trade) before drilling again. Share the lesson at the next toolbox talk.

questions.q: Which feedback from Natalie is most likely to help Joel improve his panel wiring?
o: Your panel wiring is a mess and must get much better
Good job overall; just try to be more careful next time
Your runs are neat; three ferrules don't match sheet 4
The ferrules are wrong again, as they always seem to be
questions.why: Constructive feedback is specific, about the work rather than the person, says what is good as well as what to fix, and is given soon. 'Three ferrules don't match sheet 4' tells Joel exactly what to check; vague praise or blame gives him nothing to act on.

questions.q: What should Natalie do about Joel testing for dead without proving his tester?
o: Say nothing for now, as he is new and still finding his feet
Mention it at his review at the end of his first three months
Prove the tester for him, so that his work goes a bit faster
Stop him at once, explain why, and check his next isolations
questions.why: A tester that has failed shows 'no voltage' on a live circuit, so this step is stopped at once, every time, with the reason, and then checked. Feedback months later is too late for a safety step. If he still skips it after coaching, Natalie reports it to the team leader.

questions.q: Which of these is a 'leading' safety measure, one that warns of problems before anyone is hurt?
o: Lost-time injuries this year
Near misses reported each month
Cost of injury claims paid out
Days lost through injury last month
questions.why: Leading measures track what happens before harm: near misses reported, toolbox talks held, inspections done. Lagging measures count harm after it has happened. A rise in near-miss reports often means people feel safe to report, which is good.

questions.q: A crew's start-of-day meeting often runs 40 minutes and wanders off the point. Which change would help most?
o: A set agenda, a time limit and named actions
Cancel it, and send each member a text message instead
Let whoever arrives first choose the topics each day
Move it to the end of the day, after the work is done
questions.why: A short meeting with a fixed agenda (yesterday, today's tasks, hazards and locks, materials, issues), a time limit and named actions keeps everyone on the same plan. Texts cannot check understanding, and a meeting after work cannot brief the day's hazards.
